classification.difficultyReason: Directly apply the taught tens-and-units stem-and-leaf method, order the leaves and identify the stem with the most observations.

questions.mappingNote: Part a directly assesses constructing a single-dataset stem-and-leaf plot; part b interprets the frequency of each tens group.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 Example 1 uses the tens digit as the stem, orders units-digit leaves and supplies a key. Page 3 Example 2 counts leaves by stem; page 4 demonstrates interpretation of stem-and-leaf displays.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Directly apply the taught tens-and-units stem-and-leaf method, order the leaves and identify the stem with the most observations.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the explicitly taught stem-and-leaf construction to weights and count observations within stated bounds.

questions.mappingNote: Constructing the weight plot directly uses Example 2's method for values with different numbers of digits; the remaining parts count selected leaves.
questions.methodNote: Examples 1 and 2 separate stems and leaves, order leaves and supply a key. Example 3 counts leaves satisfying specified bounds.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply the explicitly taught stem-and-leaf construction to weights and count observations within stated bounds.

classification.difficultyReason: Count selected leaves and connect the difference between extreme journey durations to departure times for a common arrival time.

questions.mappingNote: The travel-time plot supports total and interval counts. Comparing its extremes supplies the duration difference needed for the departure-time conclusion.
questions.methodNote: Use the key to read values, count qualifying leaves as in Example 3, and identify maximum and minimum values as in Example 4.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Count selected leaves and connect the difference between extreme journey durations to departure times for a common arrival time.

classification.difficultyReason: Interpret decimal-valued leaves, count strict-threshold cases and express a qualifying frequency as a percentage of the sample.

questions.mappingNote: Inflation rates use the same decimal place-value reading and frequency-to-percentage method. The original key is inconsistent and is retained for the explicitly requested independent review.
questions.methodNote: Example 4 reads decimal-valued stems and leaves and calculates a percentage as qualifying frequency divided by total frequency times 100%.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Interpret decimal-valued leaves, count strict-threshold cases and express a qualifying frequency as a percentage of the sample.

classification.difficultyReason: Read qualifying scores from a back-to-back plot and express their frequencies as percentages of 16.

questions.mappingNote: Each response reads the appropriate test's leaves, counts the scores satisfying the stated boundary and applies the percentage method demonstrated in Example 4.
questions.methodNote: Examples 1–2 explain stems and leaves. Example 3 counts scores in a back-to-back plot. Example 4 calculates a percentage by dividing the qualifying frequency by the total and multiplying by 100%.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Read qualifying scores from a back-to-back plot and express their frequencies as percentages of 16.

classification.difficultyReason: Construct a back-to-back plot from two datasets and compare their age distributions.

questions.mappingNote: Construction assesses representing data; comparison uses age groups and spread visible in the completed plot.
questions.methodNote: Use tens as stems and units as leaves. Back-to-back plots share stems, with left leaves descending on the page and right leaves ascending. Example 4 compares values and counts read from a back-to-back plot.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct a back-to-back plot from two datasets and compare their age distributions.

classification.difficultyReason: Complete a split-stem back-to-back plot and compare counts across kick thresholds.

questions.mappingNote: The question scaffold indicates the split-stem convention, but independent prior teaching evidence for this construction method is missing; method compatibility remains unresolved.
questions.methodNote: Pages 2–4 establish ordinary and back-to-back stem-and-leaf plots and counting observations. They do not demonstrate splitting each stem into rows for leaves 0–4 and 5–9.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Complete a split-stem back-to-back plot and compare counts across kick thresholds.

classification.difficultyReason: Link familiar plot-reading procedures to percentages, descending ranks and ranges across two datasets.

questions.mappingNote: The supplied weight plot uses the same back-to-back reading method. Percentages use counts from the appropriate side; the requested weight differences use its extreme observations. Ranking extends the demonstrated reading and counting method without replacing the plot with a different representation.
questions.methodNote: Read each value using the stem, leaf and key. Page 3 Example 3 counts observations meeting a condition. Page 4 Example 4 reads maxima and minima and calculates a percentage as count divided by total, multiplied by 100%. Obtain descending ranks by counting individual leaves from the largest value.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Link familiar plot-reading procedures to percentages, descending ranks and ranges across two datasets.

classification.difficultyReason: Collect comparable numerical data and organise the two datasets in a back-to-back stem-and-leaf plot.

questions.mappingNote: Question 9 directly requires collecting class data and constructing a back-to-back stem-and-leaf plot. Representing data is the primary assessed skill; collecting data is secondary.
questions.methodNote: Use the leading digits as the stem and the final digit as the leaf. Compare two numerical datasets using common stems, opposite leaf columns and a key specifying the values and units.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Collect comparable numerical data and organise the two datasets in a back-to-back stem-and-leaf plot.

classification.difficultyReason: Construct a grouped frequency table using prescribed intervals and combine its frequencies.

questions.mappingNote: Constructing and interpreting a grouped frequency table directly matches grouped-data. Example 5 is visible on supplied PDF page 7.
questions.methodNote: Example 5 groups observations into prescribed class intervals and records their frequencies. Choice of classes explains convenient equal-width intervals; requested counts are obtained by combining the relevant frequencies.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct a grouped frequency table using prescribed intervals and combine its frequencies.

classification.difficultyReason: Count observations into the explicitly supplied equal-width intervals and repeat with wider intervals; neither part requires choosing a grouping strategy.

questions.mappingNote: Both parts directly assess constructing grouped frequency tables with specified intervals; grouped-data is the closest catalogue skill.
questions.methodNote: Example 5 groups raw observations into class intervals and records their frequencies. Choice of classes explains equal-width intervals and frequencies as counts.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Count observations into the explicitly supplied equal-width intervals and repeat with wider intervals; neither part requires choosing a grouping strategy.

classification.difficultyReason: Choose convenient equal-width intervals covering the given age range for two specified numbers of classes.

questions.mappingNote: The question requires choosing suitable class intervals rather than counting observations into supplied intervals; grouped-data directly covers this task.
questions.methodNote: Example 5 demonstrates grouping observations into class intervals. Choice of classes recommends a sensible number of classes, equal widths and convenient decimal-system endpoints.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Choose convenient equal-width intervals covering the given age range for two specified numbers of classes.

classification.difficultyReason: Choose a convenient equal class width and starting point to cover the given price range in exactly eight classes.

questions.mappingNote: Question 4 applies the choice-of-classes guidance to house prices: select eight classes without constructing frequencies, since individual sale prices are not supplied.
questions.methodNote: Choose systematic, convenient class intervals of equal width that cover the complete data range.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Choose a convenient equal class width and starting point to cover the given price range in exactly eight classes.

classification.difficultyReason: Add frequencies for complete intervals and explain why a threshold within a class prevents an exact count.

questions.mappingNote: Question 5 requires reading and summing grouped frequencies, then explaining the information lost when a threshold falls inside a class. The closest catalogue skill is grouped-data.
questions.methodNote: Example 5 defines frequency as the number of data items in a class and demonstrates a grouped frequency table. Choice of classes explains intervals and class boundaries. Sum frequencies of complete requested classes; grouping does not retain individual values within a class.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Add frequencies for complete intervals and explain why a threshold within a class prevents an exact count.

classification.difficultyReason: Construct a grouped frequency table and interpret class boundaries for measurements recorded to the nearest millimetre.

questions.mappingNote: Part a applies frequency-table construction. Parts b and c interpret class membership using the stated nearest-millimetre recording precision.
questions.methodNote: Example 5 groups raw values into equal-width classes and counts their frequencies. Page 8 explains class boundaries for measurements rounded to the nearest unit.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct a grouped frequency table and interpret class boundaries for measurements recorded to the nearest millimetre.

classification.difficultyReason: Construct a categorical column graph directly from four supplied frequencies.

questions.mappingNote: The eye-colour counts require the same column-graph construction.
questions.methodNote: Example 8 constructs separated equal-width columns with labelled categorical and numerical axes.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct a categorical column graph directly from four supplied frequencies.

classification.difficultyReason: Transfer four percentages from a table to a labelled column graph.

questions.mappingNote: Channel numbers identify categories; column heights represent percentages.
questions.methodNote: Example 8 transfers tabulated category values to separated columns.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Transfer four percentages from a table to a labelled column graph.

classification.difficultyReason: Tally the five integer visit values and stack one dot per observation on a labelled number line; this directly applies the taught dot-plot method.

questions.mappingNote: The visits are discrete numerical observations suited to the demonstrated dot plot.
questions.methodNote: Example 9 stacks one dot for each observation above its numerical value.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Tally the five integer visit values and stack one dot per observation on a labelled number line; this directly applies the taught dot-plot method.

classification.difficultyReason: Construct a column graph from four tabulated categorical frequencies.

questions.mappingNote: The food categories and tabulated counts directly match that construction method.
questions.methodNote: Example 8 uses separated columns and a many-to-one numerical scale.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct a column graph from four tabulated categorical frequencies.

classification.difficultyReason: Construct a dot plot from a short list of integer observations.

questions.mappingNote: Question 5 applies that dot-plot method to integer ages.
questions.methodNote: Example 9 uses an equally spaced numerical axis and vertically stacked dots, one for each observation.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct a dot plot from a short list of integer observations.

classification.difficultyReason: Choose a frequency scale and transfer the supplied equal-width classes and frequencies to touching columns; no regrouping or inference is required.

questions.mappingNote: Question 6 explicitly references Example 6 and supplies equal-width integer-score classes, so its histogram follows that displayed tick convention.
questions.methodNote: Page 8 explains equal-width classes. Page 10 Example 6 constructs touching frequency columns; its note specifies the integer-valued convention in which ticks 40 and 50 bound the displayed class 40–49.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Choose a frequency scale and transfer the supplied equal-width classes and frequencies to touching columns; no regrouping or inference is required.

classification.difficultyReason: Group raw measurements using two specified class widths and construct histograms.

questions.mappingNote: Directly assesses grouping measurements and constructing histograms with two class widths.
questions.methodNote: Count observations into equal-width classes and draw touching frequency columns; retain the textbook's lower-class-limit horizontal labels.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Group raw measurements using two specified class widths and construct histograms.

classification.difficultyReason: Read grouped frequencies, combine classes and calculate exact percentages.

questions.mappingNote: Histogram interpretation is the principal task; percentage conversion is secondary.
questions.methodNote: Read column heights as class frequencies and combine relevant classes. Percentages express the selected frequency as a fraction of the total.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Read grouped frequencies, combine classes and calculate exact percentages.

classification.difficultyReason: Convert a stem-and-leaf plot to grouped frequencies and explain information lost by grouping.

questions.mappingNote: Combines stem-and-leaf interpretation with histogram construction and the limitation explicitly stated on page 11.
questions.methodNote: Interpret stems and leaves, count leaves into classes and construct touching columns. Grouping conceals individual values.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Convert a stem-and-leaf plot to grouped frequencies and explain information lost by grouping.

classification.difficultyReason: Interpret grouped counts and derive minimum and maximum possible totals using integer class endpoints.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–c follow the supplied histogram-reading context. Part d extends it to endpoint-weighted totals; no explicit worked demonstration of that extension occurs in the inspected teaching evidence.
questions.methodNote: Read class frequencies using the integer class convention on page 10. Page 11 explains that grouped displays conceal individual values. For bounds, use the smallest or largest integer in each class and multiply by its frequency.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Interpret grouped counts and derive minimum and maximum possible totals using integer class endpoints.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine percentage frequencies across classes and convert percentages to numbers of houses.

questions.mappingNote: Graph interpretation is the central task; part b additionally requires finding a percentage of 420.
questions.methodNote: Read and combine frequencies for the relevant classes. Example 4 calculates a percentage from a count; pages 10–11 demonstrate histogram construction and reading.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine percentage frequencies across classes and convert percentages to numbers of houses.

classification.difficultyReason: Round a measured time to identify its class and construct a histogram from grouped frequencies.

questions.mappingNote: The requested construction follows Example 6 and the grouped histogram on page 11.
questions.methodNote: Round continuous measurements to the stated precision, identify their recorded class, then use touching histogram columns with class frequencies as heights.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Round a measured time to identify its class and construct a histogram from grouped frequencies.

classification.difficultyReason: Collect two experimental datasets, represent them in two ways, compare them and suggest an alternative procedure.

questions.mappingNote: The practical procedure supplies the collection method. The directly assessed mathematical work is representing and comparing the two collected datasets.
questions.methodNote: Use ordered leaves and an explicit key for stem-and-leaf plots; group numerical readings into classes and draw touching histogram columns.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Collect two experimental datasets, represent them in two ways, compare them and suggest an alternative procedure.

classification.difficultyReason: Direct calculation of the mean and identification of the most frequent value in two short numerical lists.

questions.mappingNote: Both parts directly apply the taught mean calculation and highest-frequency definition of mode to ungrouped numerical lists. No reverse-mean or advanced statistical method is required.
questions.methodNote: Page 17 defines the mean as the sum divided by the number of values and Example 10 demonstrates substitution, summation and division. Pages 20–21 define the mode as the value with the highest frequency. Pages 2, 18 and 22 were inspected as supporting context.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct calculation of the mean and identification of the most frequent value in two short numerical lists.

classification.difficultyReason: Directly calculate the arithmetic mean of thirteen listed observations.

questions.mappingNote: This question applies the same arithmetic-mean procedure to thirteen weekly kick counts.
questions.methodNote: The Mean definition and Example 10 add all observations and divide by the number of observations, retaining the exact quotient before rounding.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Directly calculate the arithmetic mean of thirteen listed observations.

classification.difficultyReason: Decode a stem-and-leaf plot, calculate its mean and reason about an additional observation.

questions.mappingNote: The main calculation is a mean from individual marks represented by a stem-and-leaf plot. Part b counts values exceeding that mean; part c assesses the effect of adding a value above the mean.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 explains reading stems and leaves using a key. Page 17 defines the mean as the sum of values divided by their number and demonstrates substitution followed by division. Page 22 explains that larger observations increase the mean. Parts a–c use these methods, with a direct mean-formula check for the added observation.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Decode a stem-and-leaf plot, calculate its mean and reason about an additional observation.

classification.difficultyReason: Calculate a frequency-weighted mean and use it to identify and count scores below the average.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–d use a supplied frequency table to total frequencies, calculate the weighted mean, count observations below that mean and identify the modal score. The frequency-table summary-statistics skill is the closest and most advanced directly assessed catalogue skill.
questions.methodNote: Pages 17–18, Example 11, calculate a frequency-weighted mean by multiplying each value by its frequency, summing these products and dividing by the total frequency. Pages 20–21 define the mode as the value with the highest frequency; Example 15 applies both methods to a frequency table.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Calculate a frequency-weighted mean and use it to identify and count scores below the average.

classification.difficultyReason: Recover the original total from a mean, add a new observation and divide by the updated group size.

questions.mappingNote: The question requires recovering the five people's total weight from their mean before calculating the six-person mean, so find-value-from-mean is the closest directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Page 17 defines mean as the sum of values divided by their number and demonstrates substitution and division. Pages 18 and 21 demonstrate totals and means with frequencies. The inspected pages do not explicitly demonstrate recovering a total from a given mean.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recover the original total from a mean, add a new observation and divide by the updated group size.

classification.difficultyReason: Reconstruct totals from target means and carry the fifth-innings total into a dependent season-total calculation.

questions.mappingNote: Part a directly applies the taught mean formula. Parts b and c require reconstructing totals from means; find-value-from-mean is the most advanced directly assessed catalogue skill. Part c depends on the five-innings total established in part b; this gives 390 rather than subtracting only the original four-innings total.
questions.methodNote: Page 17 defines the mean as the sum divided by the number of values and demonstrates direct substitution in Example 10. Pages 18 and 21 demonstrate frequency-weighted means. The inspected pages do not explicitly demonstrate reconstructing a total from a mean or finding a target score.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Reconstruct totals from target means and carry the fifth-innings total into a dependent season-total calculation.

classification.difficultyReason: Recover two totals from their means and combine groups of unequal sizes before calculating the overall mean.

questions.mappingNote: The directly assessed result is an overall mean. Recovering each group total from its mean is a supporting reverse-mean step; the solution combines totals rather than averaging the two means.
questions.methodNote: Page 17 defines mean as sum of values divided by number of values. Pages 18 and 21 demonstrate calculating totals and dividing by the total frequency. None of the inspected pages explicitly demonstrates recovering group totals from given means and combining unequal-sized groups.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recover two totals from their means and combine groups of unequal sizes before calculating the overall mean.

classification.difficultyReason: Compare added observations with the original mean, including the combined effect of two observations on opposite sides of the mean.

questions.mappingNote: All three parts directly assess the effect of adding observations on the mean. The inspected teaching supports the mean calculation and qualitative effect of large values, but does not explicitly demonstrate the general added-observation comparison rule.
questions.methodNote: Page 17 defines mean as the sum divided by the number of values; pages 18 and 21 demonstrate means from frequency totals. Page 22 explains the effect of unusually large values on the mean. The solutions use comparison with the original mean, and part c first calculates the mean of the two added values.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Compare added observations with the original mean, including the combined effect of two observations on opposite sides of the mean.

classification.difficultyReason: Order explicitly listed data and identify the middle value or average the two middle values.

questions.mappingNote: All four parts directly apply the median definition on page 18 and the odd/even demonstrations in Example 12 on page 19.
questions.methodNote: Arrange values in numerical order. For an odd number of values select the middle value; for an even number average the two middle values.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Order explicitly listed data and identify the middle value or average the two middle values.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the median-position rule in both directions to complete a paired table.

questions.mappingNote: The assigned table applies the stated position rule directly and reverses it to recover the number of values.
questions.methodNote: Use the position (n+1)/2 in an ordered dataset; for even counts average the two middle values. Page 18 states the position rule and page 19 demonstrates odd and even medians.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply the median-position rule in both directions to complete a paired table.

classification.difficultyReason: Count the leaves in each row and locate the two middle observations using the cumulative frequencies.

questions.mappingNote: The task directly assesses finding a median from a frequency-supported stem-and-leaf display.
questions.methodNote: Count leaves to obtain row frequencies. For an even number of ordered observations, average the two middle values; Example 13 demonstrates locating a median in a stem-and-leaf display.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Count the leaves in each row and locate the two middle observations using the cumulative frequencies.

classification.difficultyReason: Read frequencies from a column graph and use cumulative counts to locate the two middle observations.

questions.mappingNote: This question directly applies the taught column-graph median method and the highest-frequency definition of mode. The frequency-table summary-statistics skill is the closest catalogue match because frequencies, rather than a raw list, determine the middle positions.
questions.methodNote: Example 14 on page 20 sums column frequencies and locates the two middle observations using cumulative frequencies. Pages 18–19 define the median and averaging of two middle values. The mode definition on page 20 and Example 15 on page 21 identify all values sharing the highest frequency.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Read frequencies from a column graph and use cumulative counts to locate the two middle observations.

classification.difficultyReason: Reason symbolically about changes to the middle values, total and number of observations.

questions.mappingNote: All six parts apply these definitions to changes in an ordered symbolic dataset. The inspected teaching pages do not explicitly demonstrate symbolic changes to mean and median; independent method compatibility remains unresolved.
questions.methodNote: Use the middle value or average of the two middle values in numerical order for the median, and total divided by the number of values for the mean. Page 22 discusses the effect of extreme values on the mean.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Reason symbolically about changes to the middle values, total and number of observations.

classification.difficultyReason: Construct an ordered dataset satisfying simultaneous mean and median constraints, choosing suitable middle values before determining the remaining age.

questions.mappingNote: Reverse the mean calculation from page 17 to obtain the required total, then apply the even-sized median procedure demonstrated on pages 18–19. Pages 21–22 distinguish measures of centre and explain their differing behaviour.
questions.methodNote: Mean is the sum divided by the number of values. For four ordered values, the median is the average of the two middle values.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct an ordered dataset satisfying simultaneous mean and median constraints, choosing suitable middle values before determining the remaining age.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise two prominent peaks, the direction of each long tail and mirrored bar heights in four supplied histograms using the taught distribution vocabulary.

questions.mappingNote: Each part requires recognition of a supplied distribution, without calculation. Shape of distribution is the primary skill; identifying the two prominent peaks in part a also assesses modality.
questions.methodNote: Page 21 introduces bimodal data through two modes and compares symmetrical and bimodal histograms. Page 22 identifies negative skew by a long left tail and positive skew by a long right tail.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recognise two prominent peaks, the direction of each long tail and mirrored bar heights in four supplied histograms using the taught distribution vocabulary.

classification.difficultyReason: Read ordered stem-and-leaf data, apply the odd and even median procedures, calculate range and mean, and identify the direction of skew.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a and b apply the mean and median methods from pages 17–19 and the range definition on page 21 to ordered stem-and-leaf plots. Part c applies the negative-skew description on page 22.
questions.methodNote: Find the mean by dividing the sum by the number of values. Use the middle ordered value for an odd number of values and average the two middle values for an even number. Find the range by subtracting the smallest value from the largest. A negatively skewed distribution has a longer tail towards lower values.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Read ordered stem-and-leaf data, apply the odd and even median procedures, calculate range and mean, and identify the direction of skew.

classification.difficultyReason: Connect the mean above the median and the large salary range to a likely long upper tail, using the taught salary example.

questions.mappingNote: The question requires predicting a likely histogram shape from summary statistics rather than calculating those statistics. Relating skew to measures of centre is the primary assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Pages 17–19 explain mean and median; page 21 defines range. Page 22 identifies positive skew by its long right tail and explains how unusually high salaries pull the mean above the median.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Connect the mean above the median and the large salary range to a likely long upper tail, using the taught salary example.

classification.difficultyReason: Select and justify suitable data-collection techniques for three different populations.

questions.mappingNote: Each discussion prompt asks how data could be collected to answer a statistical question. Sample responses apply the planning and collection stages without inventing numerical results.
questions.methodNote: Create initial questions, identify issues and plan data collection, collect and check data, then interpret findings in context.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Select and justify suitable data-collection techniques for three different populations.

classification.difficultyReason: Plan suitable surveys for different purposes and account for the intended population and response reliability.

questions.mappingNote: The three issues require collection plans rather than numerical answers. Sample solutions identify relevant respondents, suitable collection methods and practical checks on the resulting data.
questions.methodNote: Identify the statistical issue, plan collection, collect and check relevant data, and interpret it in context.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Plan suitable surveys for different purposes and account for the intended population and response reliability.

classification.difficultyReason: Read two datasets from a shared plot, calculate percentages and summary statistics, and compare distribution shapes.

questions.mappingNote: The question compares two datasets using measures, with supporting percentage and shape calculations. Pages 19–21 demonstrate ordered positions and frequency-based measures; pages 21–22 illustrate distribution shapes.
questions.methodNote: Read each leaf with its central stem; count relevant leaves and divide by the class total for percentages. Use maximum minus minimum, central ordered values, sum divided by count, and distribution shape.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Read two datasets from a shared plot, calculate percentages and summary statistics, and compare distribution shapes.

classification.difficultyReason: Convert tallies to frequencies, construct a labelled categorical display, and evaluate measures for ordered categories.

questions.mappingNote: Representing the categorical dataset is the principal construction task. The diagnosed correction limits part e to the mean because ordered size categories admit a median.
questions.methodNote: Count tally groups, identify the most frequent category, calculate a proportion as a percentage, and construct a separated-bar categorical display. Mean requires numerical values.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Convert tallies to frequencies, construct a labelled categorical display, and evaluate measures for ordered categories.

classification.difficultyReason: Link histogram frequencies to totals and percentages, use cumulative counts to locate the median class, and explain how the upper tail affects the mean relative to the median.

questions.mappingNote: Relating positive skew to mean and median is the most advanced directly assessed skill. Pages 19–20 teach median positions and frequency counting; page 22 explains upper outliers raising the mean. No inspected example explicitly demonstrates a median class for grouped prices.
questions.methodNote: Read frequencies from bar heights, sum them, calculate the relevant fraction as a percentage, use ordered positions and cumulative counts for the median class, and identify the upper tail and its effect on the mean.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Link histogram frequencies to totals and percentages, use cumulative counts to locate the median class, and explain how the upper tail affects the mean relative to the median.

classification.difficultyReason: Reverse a target mean, then determine where an unknown sixth mark must lie in the ordered data before using the middle-pair median equation.

questions.mappingNote: Part a applies the demonstrated mean calculation. Parts b and c reverse the mean and median definitions; no explicit reverse-method worked example is present in the supplied teaching evidence. Finding a value from a target mean is the closest catalogue skill, with median calculation secondary.
questions.methodNote: Page 17 calculates the mean as the sum divided by the number of values. Page 18 orders data and averages the middle two values for an even-sized set.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Reverse a target mean, then determine where an unknown sixth mark must lie in the ordered data before using the middle-pair median equation.

classification.difficultyReason: Use the supplied population-centre definition to treat city populations as frequencies and calculate separate weighted means for latitude and longitude.

questions.mappingNote: City populations act as frequencies and coordinates as numerical values. Frequency-weighted summary statistics is the closest catalogue skill; the question supplies the required coordinates.
questions.methodNote: Use the ordinary mean for one person in each city and the frequency-weighted mean demonstrated in Example 11 for unequal populations. Page 29 defines population centre and requests one decimal place.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Use the supplied population-centre definition to treat city populations as frequencies and calculate separate weighted means for latitude and longitude.

classification.difficultyReason: Select the requested cities from the supplied table, calculate population-weighted means for both coordinates, and locate the final coordinate pair on a map using the established model.

questions.mappingNote: The directly assessed calculation is a frequency-weighted mean for each coordinate. Part e also requires locating a coordinate pair on an Australian map.
questions.methodNote: Example 11 divides the sum of value times frequency by total frequency. Apply that method separately to southern latitudes and eastern longitudes, using populations as frequencies. Page 29 defines the coordinate-average population-centre model and specifies 1 decimal place.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Select the requested cities from the supplied table, calculate population-weighted means for both coordinates, and locate the final coordinate pair on a map using the established model.

classification.difficultyReason: Students must translate an average over people into two population-weighted coordinate means, relate the direction of movement to changes in cities’ population shares, and choose a defensible way to extrapolate both coordinates to 2005.

questions.mappingNote: Weighted means support the nine yearly centres and interpreting their movement. Part b requires extrapolation; interpret-linear-model is the closest catalogue skill for that most advanced directly assessed demand.
questions.methodNote: Use Example 11's frequency-weighted mean separately for latitude and longitude, following page 29's population-centre definition. The supplied teaching does not demonstrate time-trend extrapolation.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply frequency-weighted means to two coordinates, interpret their movement and choose a constant-rate extrapolation for 2005 without a supplied extrapolation procedure.

existingTransferReview.note: Decision 2 (James, 11 November 2026): published on the recorded review covering each question's current content; no new model review.

bankProjection.note: Source-confirmed category headings are omitted only from bank prompts and presentation. Explicit equivalent fraction notation repairs satisfy bank validation. Source booklet content and all questions are retained.
